text: Welcome to another episode of This is My Architecture. We're live here in Sydney again
this afternoon with a great buzz. Rob from AWS here and joining me today is Greg Coburn,
Chief Cloud Officer at AC3. Welcome, Greg. Great to have you here.
Thanks, Rob, and thanks for having me. It's an awesome day.
Yeah. Can you tell us a little bit more about what AC3 does?
Yeah. AC3 is a premier consulting partner of AWS, and we've got our MSP competency,
our digital customer experience competency, and our DevOps competency, and we help people on their cloud journey.
Awesome. And can you tell me more about the business problem we're going to be discussing here that you helped solve?
Yeah, sure. So we had New South Spatial Services kind of have this very manual process.
They had all these development applications coming in that they had to convert from GeoTIFF into LandXML.
That's provided by a third party, and they were keeping track of this conversion with spreadsheets,
and when they had inquiries coming in, it was all a very manual process and very slow for them.
All right. So converting a very manual process into what I understand to be a completely serverless process.
So can you draw us or walk us through it, please?
Yeah, no trouble. So we might have a developer come in here, and they need to talk to API Gateway, right?
So we've got our GeoTIFF that comes in there. It goes in from API Gateway, and it'll get stored into S3.
Yep.
From there, it triggers a notification to our third-party provider here.
Cool.
So that GeoTIFF file will get sent over to that third-party provider.
They'll then send back what's called a LandXML file, and a LandXML file is a representation of that TIFF
in a particular format that has some geospatial information.
From there, we need to kick off the validation process here.
Cool. And how are you kicking that step function off?
That step function is kicked off by an event. So when that file lands in S3 bucket with the right folder structure,
the step function gets kicked off.
So then from there, we start off by doing a very simple, is this valid XML, right?
So step function is many Lambda functions, and we're able to parallelize that out, right?
So we check, is that a valid XML, and is it currently conforming to the current LandXML format?
And what kind of libraries and technologies are you using to do that inside of Lambda?
Yeah. So over here, we actually do our render validation over here, okay?
So this one is actually forming a polygon, and we had to use the geospatial libraries
that were provided along with Python to do that, okay?
So the problem that we had there, the challenge that we faced with that was those objects were really, really big, okay?
And the package size that you can have for Lambda is actually kind of small.
So we had to kind of understand what was in those shared objects and all the relationship there that we needed
to only get us down to the core that we needed to draw those polygons in memory
and get that into a size that was available and usable by Lambda.
And so this is ultimately why you've ended up splitting things out to get that library size down?
Correct, correct.
Okay, cool. So you validated your polygons, you know, around the boundaries of the property.
What are you doing with that data next?
Yeah, so what we do with that data is we're actually storing that all into DynamoDB.
So there's a whole bunch of these validations that kick off.
Yep.
And depending on what's happening, they might store different information and some might fail and some might succeed.
And that's all interesting for different people.
And based on who it is, we might get a notification center out here and it might alert someone to where it is in the process
or if there was a broken step in that validation that they need to go and get rectified or something like that.
Okay. And are you using step functions to manage your state exclusively or is there some state stored in Dynamo?
There's a little bit of both depending on a number of things.
So we've got state stored in step functions for the validation process.
But the document can actually go through a number of iterations, right?
So a developer might need to upload another document, another version of that document,
and that particular state is being stored in DynamoDB.
And using exactly the same workflow to update and represent that state.
So imagine you've actually got multiple developers uploading things several times.
We can actually take this whole process here and parallelize that again, right?
So we've not got just the parallelization process within the step functions.
We can parallelize that step function process again as well.
Okay.
So what's the net result of this for the business?
You've gone from what I understand would take multiple days to how long would this?
We can now do up to 500 documents a day that we're processing through the system.
We're doing now 250 validations, which we were never able to do before, on that land XML.
So all sorts of things that they're checking.
And it's up to two days faster now for that process to get that geotiff file converted into that land XML.
That is an absolutely awesome result.
Thank you so much, Greg, for coming and explaining what you've done
to build the world's first serverless geospatial data lake.
And thank you very much for listening to another episode of This is My Architecture.
Thanks, Rob.
Back to the desk.
